claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 in high-temperature oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by breakdown of a surface oxide scale.
The alloy initially forms a thin, protective oxide scale enriched predominantly in Cr and Ti, with a minor Al contribution.
The initial Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale is coherent and limits oxygen ingress.
Prolonged thermal exposure causes the oxide scale to lose coherency through spallation, thickening, or phase transformation.
Oxide-scale instability permits internal oxidation and localized microstructural damage.
The starting additively manufactured alloy has a single-phase fcc microstructure.
The starting alloy demonstrates high strength.
The starting alloy demonstrates high fatigue performance.
Gas composition modulates oxide-instability kinetics and the resulting degradation pathway.
Under oxidizing gas, the alloy will exhibit an initial period of slow weight gain caused by protective oxide formation.
After the initial slow-growth period in oxidizing gas, oxide breakdown will produce accelerated degradation.
Reducing conditions may delay complete oxide spallation relative to oxidizing conditions.
Internal oxidation can still occur under the proposed reducing conditions.
Oxide breakdown and internal oxidation will correlate with reductions in tensile strength and fatigue life.
At comparable temperatures in an inert or low-reactivity environment, the fcc matrix and thin native oxide will remain stable.
The proposed degradation mechanism is active between approximately 600 and 900 degrees Celsius when gas composition supplies sufficient chemical driving force.
The proposed exposure range remains below the threshold for complete phase transformation of the alloy.
Comparing oxygen-rich, hydrogen-containing reducing, and inert atmospheres at 600, 750, and 900 degrees Celsius can distinguish the proposed mechanism.
An adherent scale with no internal oxidation or mechanical degradation would falsify oxide-scale breakdown as the degradation driver.
A lack of correlation between oxide-scale instability and performance loss would falsify the proposed mechanism.
